tagline: Roman ruins on the edge of the Sahara
overview:
Libya spreads across North Africa between Egypt and Tunisia, with a long Mediterranean coastline in the north and the Sahara Desert filling everything else. It is the fourth-largest country in Africa, about two and a half times the size of Texas, yet more than 90 percent of it is desert where almost no one lives. The capital, Tripoli, is a white city on the coast with an old walled medina, and nearly all Libyans live in a thin strip along the sea.

About 7 million people live in Libya, and Arabic is the official language; Berber (Amazigh) communities in the western mountains speak their own language, and nearly everyone is Sunni Muslim. Libya has some of the largest oil reserves in Africa, which once made it one of the continent's wealthiest countries per person. Since a 2011 uprising overthrew the dictator Muammar Gaddafi, however, rival governments and armed groups have fought for control, and daily life has often been disrupted. The country's spectacular Roman and Greek ruins and Saharan rock art remain among the finest anywhere.
landAndNature: Libya has three regions. Tripolitania in the northwest has coastal plains, olive groves, and the Nafusa Mountains, home to Berber villages and underground houses. Cyrenaica in the east rises into the green Jebel Akhdar hills, the wettest part of the country. Fezzan in the southwest is deep Sahara: the Ubari Sand Sea holds salt lakes fringed with palms between towering dunes, and the black volcanic Waw an Namus crater cradles three colored lakes. The Acacus Mountains hide rock paintings of giraffes and dancers thousands of years old. Rainfall is tiny; some desert areas may see no rain for a decade. Fennec foxes, jerboas, and desert monitors survive the heat, and the coast has some of the last untouched beaches in the Mediterranean, where loggerhead turtles nest.
peopleAndCulture: Most Libyans are Arab or mixed Arab-Berber, with Amazigh, Tuareg, and Toubou minorities in the mountains and desert, and family and tribe remain important in daily life. Meals are shared from common dishes: bazin, a hard dough of barley flour served with lamb and tomato sauce, couscous, and shorba soup, followed by dates and sweet tea with mint, often poured with froth on top. Libyan tea ceremonies can last hours. Traditional clothing includes long white robes and embroidered vests for celebrations, and weddings run for days with music from the zokra bagpipe and drums. Soccer is the favorite sport, and the national team won the African Nations Championship in 2014. Ghadames, an ancient oasis town of covered whitewashed streets, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
history: Berbers lived here for thousands of years, and Phoenicians founded Tripoli while Greeks built Cyrene in the east around 630 BC. Rome ruled for centuries and left Leptis Magna, one of the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere, birthplace of the emperor Septimius Severus. Arabs brought Islam in the 600s, and the Ottoman Empire controlled the coast from 1551. Italy invaded in 1911 and ruled brutally as a colony until World War II. Libya became an independent kingdom in 1951, and oil was discovered in 1959. In 1969 a young officer, Muammar Gaddafi, seized power and ruled as a dictator for 42 years, until an uprising and NATO airstrikes toppled him in 2011. Since then Libya has been divided between competing governments, with periods of civil war and fragile ceasefires.
funFacts: Leptis Magna, near Tripoli, is so well preserved that its Roman theater, market, and harbor still stand largely intact.
The Ubari Sand Sea has lakes in the middle of the desert that are so salty swimmers float, and their shores are lined with palms.
Libya's Great Man-Made River is one of the largest irrigation projects ever built, pumping water from deep desert aquifers to the coast.
Under Gaddafi, Libya's flag was plain green, the only single-color national flag in the world, until it changed back in 2011.
Ghadames is called the pearl of the desert; its houses connect through covered alleys so people can walk the town in the shade.
